text: In T-SQL you declared a type for every column, so a money column could never contain the text n-slash-a. Files and APIs make no such promise. When pandas reads a CSV with one stray n-slash-a, or one dollar sign in a numeric column, it plays safe and stores the whole column as text, dtype object. Sums, averages, sorting, and date arithmetic then quietly misbehave. This lesson shows how to catch wrong types and convert them safely.

Here's an illustrative raw orders table where literally everything arrived as text — an order id, a dollar-formatted amount with one n-slash-a mixed in, a date column with one not-recorded entry, and a shipped column written as Yes, No, yes, and N, all meaning the same two things. Check dtypes, and every single column comes back object — pandas' catch-all for text. Make dtypes, or the fuller info, the very first thing you run on any new dataset.

The direct approach fails loudly — try astype float on that amount column, and you get a ValueError, could not convert string to float, because of the dollar sign and comma. Strip those symbols out with a regex replace first, then convert with pd dot to underscore numeric, passing errors equals coerce. Now you get 1200.50, 75.00, NaN for the n-slash-a, and 310.25 — a clean numeric column where the one bad value became an ordinary missing value instead of crashing everything.

Pd dot to underscore datetime with errors equals coerce does the same job for dates — the three real dates convert cleanly, and the not-recorded entry becomes NaT, not a time, the date equivalent of NaN. Once the column is a genuine datetime64, you can filter by range, pull out dot-d-t dot month, and subtract dates directly.

Here's a trap worth knowing: is 03 slash 05 slash 2024 March 5th, or May 3rd? It depends entirely on the country, and pandas will not warn you either way. Parse the exact same text with percent-m slash percent-d slash percent-capital-Y, and you get March 5th; parse it with percent-d slash percent-m slash percent-capital-Y instead, and you get May 3rd. Both succeed without complaint, and only one of them is actually right — whenever you know the source's convention, pass format explicitly rather than trusting the default guess.

A few smaller conversions round this out. Astype int turns a clean id column into real integers — fine once you know there are no gaps, since a column containing NaN can't be a plain int. For booleans, normalize the text first — lowercase it and take the first letter, so Yes, yes, and Y all collapse to the same y — then map y to True and n to False. And a column with a few repeated labels, like a membership tier, can be stored as category — more compact, and it signals the values come from a fixed set. Finish by checking dtypes again to confirm every column now has the type you actually intended.

To recap: check dtypes first — object on a numeric-looking column is a red flag. Strip symbols, then pd dot to underscore numeric with errors equals coerce. Pd dot to underscore datetime with errors equals coerce gives real dates and NaT for junk, and you should state the format for any ambiguous strings. Convert flags to booleans and repeated labels to categories, and re-check types after every single change you make.
